t: What a Flexible Magnetic Pickup Tool Is
title: What a Flexible Magnetic Pickup Tool Is
description: A flexible magnetic pickup tool is a bendable shaft — usually a spring-steel coil — with a magnet on the end and a handle, made for fishing dropped screws out of PC cases. Screws fall into the worst places: behind the motherboard tray, under the PSU shroud, into front-panel crevices. The flexible shaft snakes in, the magnet grabs the screw, and you pull it out without disassembling half the build.

print("Job: dropped screws behind tray, under shroud, in crevices.")
print("Snake in, magnet grabs, pull out: no disassembly required.")

t: Telescoping vs Flexible: The Two Pickup Designs
title: Telescoping vs Flexible: The Two Pickup Designs
description: Telescoping pickup tools are rigid tubes that extend 24 to 36 inches — great for straight-line reaches into deep cases. Flexible tools bend around corners and through cable nests where rigid tubes cannot go. For PC work the flexible tool wins inside the case (everything is around a corner), while the telescoping tool wins for screws dropped behind the desk. The prepared bench has both; they cost a few dollars each.

print("Telescoping: rigid, 24-36 in reach, straight lines (behind the desk).")
print("Flexible: bends around corners, through cable nests (INSIDE the case).")
print("PC verdict: flexible for the case, telescoping for the floor. Both: a few dollars.")

t: Pull Force Ratings: What the Pounds Mean
title: Pull Force Ratings: What the Pounds Mean
description: Pickup magnets are rated by pull force — typically 1 to 5 pounds for PC-suitable tools. One to two pounds lifts any PC screw with control; five-plus pounds grabs the screw plus every nearby washer and the tool fights you in tight spaces. Stronger is not better inside a case: the right pull lifts the target without collecting the neighborhood.

print("5+ lb: grabs screw + washers + fights you in tight spaces.")
print("Inside a case, stronger is NOT better: control beats force.")

t: Shaft Lengths and Diameters for Case Work
title: Shaft Lengths and Diameters for Case Work
description: The useful flexible length is 18 to 24 inches — long enough to reach from the case mouth to the farthest corner, short enough to control. Shaft diameter around 1/4 inch fits through cable routing holes and beside GPU brackets; thicker shafts cannot pass the gaps where screws actually hide. A slim long shaft beats a thick short one for every real retrieval.

title: Technique: The Slow Sweep Retrieval
description: Do not stab at the screw — sweep slowly. Feed the shaft in with the magnet leading, move it in slow arcs across the area, and feel for the magnetic tug that says contact. Once it grabs, pull straight out along the entry path; yanking sideways drops the screw again. If the screw is visible, guide the magnet to it; if not, sweep the whole zone methodically like a metal detector.

t: Retrieval Scenario: Screw Behind the Motherboard Tray
title: Retrieval Scenario: Screw Behind the Motherboard Tray
description: The classic: a standoff screw slips and falls behind the tray where fingers cannot reach. Feed the flexible shaft through the nearest cable routing hole, sweep the tray's back channel slowly, and listen for the click of contact. Pull the shaft back through the same hole. Total time: under a minute. Without the tool: removing the motherboard.

t: Retrieval Scenario: Screw Under the PSU Shroud
title: Retrieval Scenario: Screw Under the PSU Shroud
description: PSU shrouds create a dark cave where screws vanish. Slide the shaft under the shroud's edge, sweep the floor of the compartment, and retrieve without removing the shroud or PSU. Tip: shine the headlamp into the gap first — if you can see the screw, one guided pass does it; blind sweeping takes longer but still works.

t: Retrieval Scenario: Dropped in the Front-Panel Cavity
title: Retrieval Scenario: Dropped in the Front-Panel Cavity
description: Front-panel cavities and drive cages swallow screws into narrow vertical slots. The flexible shaft's bend is the answer: curve the tip, feed it down the slot, and let the magnet find the screw at the bottom. A telescoping rigid tool cannot make this turn — this scenario is why the flexible tool exists.

t: LED Pickup Tools: Light at the Tip
title: LED Pickup Tools: Light at the Tip
description: Some pickup tools build an LED into the handle or tip, lighting the retrieval zone as you work. In a dark case interior this is genuinely useful — you see the screw and guide the magnet in one motion. The LED adds cost and battery concerns; a headlamp does the same job. Worth it if you do a lot of blind retrievals; otherwise the headlamp suffices.

t: Non-Magnetic Retrieval: When the Screw Isn't Steel
title: Non-Magnetic Retrieval: When the Screw Isn't Steel
description: Brass standoffs, aluminum screws, and plastic clips ignore magnets. For those, the pickup tool's shaft still helps — wrap a tiny piece of sticky tack on the tip, or use the shaft to push the part somewhere reachable. Long tweezers and hemostats are the real answer for non-ferrous retrieval. Know before you sweep: magnet for steel, tack or tweezers for the rest.

demo.program:
print("Magnet: steel screws only.")
print("Brass/aluminum/plastic: sticky tack on tip, or long tweezers/hemostats.")
print("Know before you sweep: match the tool to the material.")

t: Maintenance: Keeping the Magnet Strong and Clean
title: Maintenance: Keeping the Magnet Strong and Clean
description: Pickup magnets collect metal dust that weakens their effective grip — wipe the tip clean after each use. Do not store the tool stuck to steel (it slowly demagnetizes cheaper magnets) or near heat. Check pull yearly by lifting a known screw; a tool that barely holds an M3 is retired to desk duty. The shaft's spring steel needs no maintenance beyond keeping it clean.

t: Pickup Tool vs Tweezers vs Disassembly
title: Pickup Tool vs Tweezers vs Disassembly
description: Pickup tool: fastest for ferrous screws in deep spots, no disassembly. Tweezers: best for visible screws and non-ferrous parts, need line of sight. Disassembly: the last resort — guaranteed but costs 30 minutes. The hierarchy is tool first, tweezers second, disassembly never if the first two work. A 5-dollar pickup tool has saved thousands of builder-hours.

t: Buying Guide: What to Look For
title: Buying Guide: What to Look For
description: Look for: a real spring-steel flexible shaft (not floppy wire), a neodymium tip in the 1-2 lb range, a comfortable handle, and 18-plus inches of length. Avoid gimmicky multi-claw grabbers for PC work — the claws are too big for case interiors. Expect 5 to 12 dollars. Buy two: one for the bench, one for the go-bag, because drops happen on site too.

title: Advanced: Retrieval Without Scratching Components
description: A bare magnet dragged across a motherboard can scratch traces — sleeve the tip with a turn of electrical tape, leaving just the magnet face exposed. Move slowly near boards, never scrape. For screws resting on a GPU backplate, guide the magnet down vertically instead of sliding in from the side. The retrieval should never risk the board it is saving.

print("Near boards: slow, vertical approaches, never scrape.")
print("The retrieval must never risk the board it's saving.")
